    The beginnings of the growth of social sciences to a place of importance in the college curriculum is apparent in the Savoy College in such courses as Political Economy and Mental Philosophy.

Typical American College Standards of the Period.—An adequate comparative evaluation of the curriculum of Savoy College, however, requires that it be measured against standards common to its time and locale. A composite measuring stick for such purposes may be found in the following nutshell characterization of post-Civil War colleges in the United States in a historical study of American higher educational standards and attainments made by Professor Andrew Fleming West's backward look at the colleges, presented in his monograph, "The American College," written in 1909:

    . . . The American college, as contrasted with European schools, is a secondary institution, the name college notwithstanding. It enrolled boys who had passed regularly of a fourteen-year course of study leading to the bachelor's degree—or who had had four years of college-preparatory training on top of eight years of secondary education, with some anticipations of university courses toward the end of the school's duration.³⁸ But these embryonic university studies were usually taught as recitations rather than real college lectures, even in the better Eastern colleges of the time. Boys entered college when they were fifteen or sixteen years of age. The course of preparation did not often exceed twenty years. The usual course of preparation in the better schools had been a year or so in history and a year or so in natural philosophy and in chemistry, and in English and American literature was offered, and in the addition of the Classical courses was Xenophon's Anabasis and two of Homer's Iliad, together with arithmetic, and algebra to quadratics (complete) and algebra to, or at most through, quadratic equations together constituting a fair program of elementary mathematics that was a combination of Greek and mathematics specified above constituted as much as the college colleges required for en-
